=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer-side assessment

**Do not accept this as a settled or “standard” package.** The Seller’s labels, market assertions and statements that terms were agreed are not evidence of Buyer approval. Confirm any actual agreements against the Buyer’s records.

The central concern is the **combined effect**: known problems are disclosed, disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge may defeat warranty claims, and broadly drafted limitations may also restrict indemnities and other remedies. The Buyer could inherit the risks without effective recourse.

This review is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying DD documents or full SPA. The points below identify what to require and verify.

## Material issues and recommended pushback

### 1. Liability protections are too broad—and should not apply uniformly

**Seller position:** A 20% general warranty cap, AUD 25,000 de minimis, AUD 250,000 deductible basket and 18-month notification period, potentially applying across all Claims. Capacity and title receive the same protection.

**Buyer concern:** A general warranty package cannot appropriately cover every obligation. Under the proposed title regime, the Buyer could pay AUD 24 million but have recovery capped at AUD 4.8 million if the Seller cannot deliver valid ownership. Applying these limitations to completion obligations, debt discharge, tax or specific indemnities would undermine the agreed transaction.

**Push back:**
- Limit the general warranty regime expressly to defined **General Warranty Claims**.
- Give title, capacity and authority warranties a separate cap of at least the purchase price and a materially longer claim period.
- Provide separate regimes for tax and specific indemnities, tailored to their exposure and discovery periods.
- Exclude purchase-price adjustments, debt repayment, security releases and other payment/completion obligations from the general warranty cap, basket and short time limit.
- Preserve appropriate fraud and deliberate-concealment carve-outs; reject attempts to exclude liability that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- Negotiate the general warranty cap, thresholds and duration as a package. Eighteen months may leave insufficient time to discover issues through full reporting cycles. Seek a longer period, a lower de minimis and a tipping basket rather than recovery of only the excess.
- Aggregate related claims for threshold purposes.

The numerical terms are commercial negotiation points, not automatically unacceptable. **Their indiscriminate extension to other claims is the more serious problem.**

### 2. Disclosure and Buyer-knowledge provisions could remove meaningful warranty protection

**Seller position:** Everything contained or referred to in the data room, accounts, registers and public records is disclosed. Anything the Buyer or its advisers knew—or could discover—bars claims.

**Buyer concern:** This shifts the burden of identifying and understanding every risk onto the Buyer. A reference buried in a document could become a defence even where its significance was not apparent. It also treats adviser knowledge and constructive knowledge as Buyer acceptance.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure**, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter, preferably against the relevant warranty.
- Reject blanket disclosure of everything “referred to” in the data room and unrestricted public-record disclosure.
- Freeze and retain an agreed indexed copy of the disclosed data room.
- Delete the constructive-knowledge bar and automatic attribution of advisers’ knowledge. If a knowledge qualification is unavoidable, confine it to actual knowledge of named Buyer personnel, with a tightly defined scope.
- State that disclosure and Buyer knowledge do **not** qualify specific indemnities, completion obligations or other expressly protected matters.

For known issues, a warranty alone is inadequate if the issue is disclosed against it: obtain a cure, price treatment or an express indemnity.

### 3. Bluefen consent must be effective and its conditions satisfied

Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**. No final consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions is supplied.

**Buyer concern:** Reasonable endeavours are not an outcome. Delivering a consent letter may not make consent effective if clause 11.3 conditions remain outstanding or the consent imposes adverse commercial terms.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent, including satisfaction of applicable conditions, a Buyer-waivable condition precedent.
- Require consent on terms reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, without unapproved adverse changes.
- Obtain evidence of effectiveness, not merely delivery.
- Include a long-stop date and an appropriate Buyer termination right if the condition fails.

Do not conclude that consent has been “addressed” on the current evidence.

### 4. Riverlark repayment and security release belong at Completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding; no final discharge is included.

**Buyer concern:** A release promised after Completion exposes the acquired company to continuing secured debt and potentially change-of-control consequences. It is inconsistent with a debt-free acquisition unless properly resolved through the completion mechanics.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a current payoff letter covering principal, interest, fees and discharge requirements.
- Repay the facility through the completion funds flow, ordinarily from the Seller’s proceeds under the agreed price mechanics.
- Require binding lender release arrangements effective on repayment, covering all relevant security and guarantees, with prompt registration of discharges.
- Check any required change-of-control waiver for the period before discharge.

Confirm whether AUD 24 million is the headline enterprise value or fixed equity consideration and reconcile the adjustment formula. **Do not deduct the same debt twice.**

### 5. Completion bonuses must be allocated and funded expressly

DD-005 identifies **AUD 420,000** of conditional bonuses omitted from the funds flow; on-costs are unresolved.

**Buyer concern:** Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the company from bearing a payment obligation after Completion.

**Push back:**
- Review the actual entitlement, employment conditions, payer and payment timing.
- Allocate transaction-triggered bonuses expressly to the Seller economically, through payment, a price adjustment or a specific indemnity.
- Quantify applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs.
- Include the resulting amounts in the funds flow or an appropriate reserve.

Avoid double counting amounts already captured in debt, transaction expenses or working capital.

### 6. Ironquay requires proof of IP ownership—not merely a narrow payment indemnity

Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. AUD 180,000 is recorded as open, but that is **not conclusive evidence of non-payment**.

**Buyer concern:** The company may lack ownership of material software or other deliverables. An indemnity limited to the invoice amount would not necessarily cover the commercial consequences of defective title.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all SOW3 fees and obtain reliable payment evidence.
- Require any necessary payment and a confirmatory assignment, together with verification of the relevant IP chain of title.
- If material IP ownership remains unresolved, make satisfactory resolution a completion condition.
- Broaden the specific indemnity to cover losses arising from the identified ownership/payment defect, including relevant third-party claims and remediation costs—not just the SOW3 payment.
- Keep that indemnity outside general disclosure, knowledge, basket and inappropriate time-limit restrictions.

### 7. The export incident is unresolved, not established to be immaterial

The facts indicate a potential exposure involving approximately **1,240 records**, but access, scope, notification requirements and loss remain undetermined.

**Buyer concern:** Neither “confirmed breach” nor “immaterial operational matter” is justified yet. Uncertainty itself requires investigation and allocation.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the investigation record, access logs, containment steps, affected data categories and relevant privacy/security advice.
- Assess applicable legal and contractual notification requirements; do not assume notification is required or unnecessary.
- Require evidence preservation, continuing updates and appropriate pre-Completion remediation.
- Seek a tailored indemnity for the pre-Completion incident, including reasonable investigation, remediation and third-party exposure, with legally recoverable regulatory amounts addressed carefully.
- Consider a holdback or escrow if material exposure remains unresolved.

### 8. Sandbar renewals need aggregate review, not an “ordinary-course” label

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**.

**Buyer concern:** Separate AUD 110,000 commitments could obscure the aggregate obligation or evade consent thresholds. Their treatment depends on timing, service periods, termination rights and accounting—not the Seller’s label.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and establish when each commitment became binding.
- Test the aggregate against interim operating covenants and approval thresholds.
- Determine whether amounts are accrued operating liabilities, future service costs or unusual commitments.
- Agree price treatment or remediation where appropriate; do not automatically classify the entire amount as debt.

### 9. Tax and IP should not simply fall into the short general regime

**Tax:** Seek a separate pre-Completion tax covenant/indemnity, appropriate tax warranties and claim periods aligned with relevant assessment and reopening periods, with a notification buffer. Do not subject tax recovery to ordinary warranty baskets or broad disclosure qualifications.

**IP:** Preserve substantive ownership, licensing and infringement warranties, supported by diligence into contractor assignments, material licences and relevant open-source use. Set protection by reference to the business’s dependence on its IP, not the assertion that the position is settled.

### 10. The share register is evidence—not complete title assurance

DD-012 records Harbourglass as the registered holder of all shares.

**Push back:** Verify the issued capital, valid allotments and transfers, beneficial ownership, encumbrances, options and other rights to acquire shares, and any transfer restrictions or pre-emption rights. Require appropriate completion instruments and express warranties that the Buyer receives **100% of the shares free of encumbrances**.

### 11. Do not invent consent requirements for the lease or Mossvale

The supplied material identifies:
- an office lease **notification** obligation; and
- a Mossvale **assignment** restriction, not an express share-sale consent requirement.

Review the complete provisions and definitions. Require any applicable notice, but do not automatically demand landlord consent or treat a share sale as an assignment. Conversely, check for separate change-of-control provisions before concluding no consent is needed.

### 12. Exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions need targeted carve-outs

Their application to “all Claims of any nature” could cut across negotiated protections.

Require express preservation of specific indemnities, price adjustments, debt and completion obligations, and appropriate equitable relief and fraud protections. Review any statutory-claim exclusions under applicable Australian law rather than assuming they are effective.

Also check the full SPA for procedural traps: unusually detailed notification requirements, short deadlines to commence proceedings after notice, or settlement-control provisions that impair recovery.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

| Priority | Buyer position |
|---|---|
| **Completion certainty** | Effective Bluefen consent; funded Riverlark discharge; satisfactory material IP ownership evidence; verified clean share title. |
| **Price integrity** | Reconcile debt-free/cash-free mechanics; allocate bonuses and on-costs; investigate Sandbar commitments; prevent double counting. |
| **Effective recourse** | Separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow disclosure and knowledge defences; constrain all-claims limitations. |
| **Unresolved exposure** | Investigate the export incident and Ironquay position; secure tailored indemnities and consider retained proceeds where warranted. |

**Bottom line:** Do not let disclosure become a substitute for resolution. Material known risks should be cured before Completion, reflected in price, or supported by enforceable, appropriately secured recourse—not disclosed away under a universal limitation package.
